<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en-US">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Neural Fields as World Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text">Joshua Nunley (joshnunl@iu.edu)</span>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, Indiana University, Bloomington
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Cognitive Science Program, Indiana University, Bloomington
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">How does the brain predict physical outcomes while acting in the world?
Machine learning world models compress visual input into latent spaces, discarding the spatial structure that characterizes sensory cortex.
We propose isomorphic world models: architectures preserving sensory topology so that physics prediction becomes geometric propagation rather than abstract state transition.
We implement this using neural fields with motor-gated channels, where activity evolves through local lateral connectivity and motor commands multiplicatively modulate specific populations.
Three experiments support this approach: (1) local connectivity is sufficient to learn ballistic physics, with predictions traversing intermediate locations rather than “teleporting”; (2) policies trained entirely in imagination transfer to real physics at nearly twice the rate of latent-space alternatives; and (3) motor-gated channels spontaneously develop body-selective encoding through visuomotor prediction alone.
These findings suggest intuitive physics and body schema may share a common origin in spatially structured neural dynamics.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords:</span> neural fields; world models; intuitive physics; motor control; body schema</p>
  
</div>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Introduction</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A child learning to catch must solve two physics problems at once: where will
the ball land, and where will my hand be when I reach?
With practice, both predictions become automatic.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">How does the brain pull this off?
Battaglia, Hamrick, and Tenenbaum proposed that humans possess an “intuitive
physics engine” (IPE) that runs mental simulations to predict physical outcomes
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Battaglia et al., 2013</a>)</cite>.
The framework accounts for human performance across diverse physical reasoning tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hamrick et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ullman et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Several computational frameworks have attempted to model physical intuition.
Object-based approaches like Interaction Networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Battaglia et al., 2016</a>)</cite>
and the Neural Physics Engine <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chang et al., 2017</a>)</cite> learn to predict
physical dynamics over explicit object graphs.
These models capture important structure but operate on symbolic object
representations rather than raw visual input, and they do not integrate motor
commands. They model physics as an observer, not as an agent.
To understand how the brain predicts physics while acting in the world, we need
models that integrate action.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grush (2004)</a></cite> proposed that the brain constructs exactly such models: internal emulators that predict the sensory consequences of motor commands.
World models from machine learning, which learn these predictions for planning and control, can be seen as computational implementations of this idea <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018</a>)</cite>.
But these architectures ignore biological constraints.
Visual input is compressed through an encoder into a latent vector with no
spatial structure, a recurrent model predicts latent state transitions, and
finally a decoder reconstructs predictions.
In such architectures, a single weight matrix can connect any latent dimension
to any other, allowing information to jump discontinuously rather than propagate
locally.
In the physical world, a ball moves continuously through space, forces act on
adjacent objects, and trajectories unfold through spatial neighborhoods.
Latent-space world models have no such constraints.
Predicted objects can “teleport” across representational space from one timestep to the next.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Neuroscience suggests the brain does it differently.
Ahuja and colleagues showed that motion-sensitive area MT activates during
trajectory prediction even without visual motion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahuja et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahuja et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Neural patterns during prediction resemble those during actual motion
perception, as if physics simulation unfolds <span id="Sx1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">within</span> spatially organized
visual representations rather than in a separate abstract reasoning system.
The brain appears to preserve spatial structure while simulating physics.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This leaves a gap: we lack a world model architecture that respects both
constraints, spatial structure <span id="Sx1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">and</span> action integration.
If we want to understand how brains model the world, we need world models that
could plausibly exist in brains.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We propose that the missing link is <span id="Sx1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">isomorphism</span>:
world models that preserve the spatial structure of sensory input.
The defining constraint is <span id="Sx1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">locality</span>: nearby points in the world map to
nearby points in the representation, and information propagates through spatial
neighbors rather than “teleporting” via global connections.
When this constraint is enforced, physics prediction becomes a geometric
problem: a ball’s future is a path through representational space, not an
abstract vector transition.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To test this hypothesis, we use <span id="Sx1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">neural fields</span>, perhaps the simplest
implementation of the isomorphic principle.
Introduced by Amari <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amari, 1977</a>)</cite>, neural fields are spatially
organized recurrent networks where activity evolves through local lateral
interactions: each location influences only its spatial neighbors through a
connectivity kernel.
Neural fields have long served as models of cortical dynamics, capturing
phenomena from visual attention to working memory to motor planning.
Yet they have not been explored as world models, learning to predict how the world evolves for planning and control.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To enable action-conditional prediction, we introduce <span id="Sx1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">motor-gated
channels</span>: populations whose activity is multiplicatively modulated by motor
commands.
The mechanism implements gain modulation, a fundamental computational principle
in cortex whereby one signal multiplicatively scales neural responses to another
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas and Thier, 2000</a>)</cite>.
In posterior parietal cortex, gain fields enable sensorimotor integration by
combining visual input with motor signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andersen et al., 1997</a>)</cite>.
This is precisely the computation our motor-gated channels perform.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18690v1/architecture_diagram.svg" id="Sx1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/303;" width="698" height="303"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Neural field world model architecture. Visual input <math id="Sx1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is added to the hidden state only during the first three timesteps of each sequence; thereafter, the field evolves autonomously through local lateral convolution (<math id="Sx1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>) and recurrence. Motor commands <math id="Sx1.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐦</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{m}</annotation></semantics></math> multiplicatively gate specific channels, implementing gain modulation. A 1x1 convolution reconstructs the visual prediction <math id="Sx1.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{I}_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>I</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{I}_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Four lines of evidence support that this architecture implements a biologically
plausible world model:</p>
<ol id="Sx1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="Sx1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Architectural Alignment:</span> The model’s retinotopic organization
and motor-gating mechanism parallel known structures in area MT
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahuja et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and posterior parietal cortex <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas and Thier, 2000</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Sx1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Physics from Lateral Dynamics:</span> The constraint of local
connectivity proves sufficient to learn ballistic physics, where trajectories
emerge from wave-like propagation rather than symbolic rules (Experiment 1).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Sx1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transferable Motor Control:</span> Policies trained entirely in
“imagination,” within the frozen world model, transfer successfully to
real physics, suggesting the spatial representation captures actionable
structure (Experiment 2).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="Sx1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="Sx1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Emergent Body Schema:</span> Motor-gated channels spontaneously
develop body-selective encoding through sensorimotor prediction alone,
producing the motor-linked self-representation characteristic of body
schema <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gallagher, 2005</a>)</cite> (Experiment 3).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Methods</h2>

<section id="Sx2.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Neural Field Architecture</h3>

<div id="Sx2.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The neural field instantiates the key constraint motivating our approach: information propagates through spatial neighbors, never teleporting across the representation.
At each timestep, the field state <math id="Sx2.SSx1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐡</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times H\times W}</annotation></semantics></math> updates through three influences: decay of current activity, lateral input from neighboring locations, and visual input from the environment.
A learned convolutional kernel <math id="Sx2.SSx1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="Sx2.SSx1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7\times 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\times 7</annotation></semantics></math>) implements lateral connectivity, ensuring that predicted motion must traverse intermediate positions just as objects traverse intermediate locations in physical space.
Formally, the dynamics follow Amari’s neural field equations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amari, 1977</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="Sx2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{t+1}=\mathbf{h}_{t}+\frac{\Delta t}{\tau}\left(-\mathbf{h}_{t}+K*\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{h}_{t})+W_{\text{in}}*\mathbf{I}_{t}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>τ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext>ReLU</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{t+1}=\mathbf{h}_{t}+\frac{\Delta t}{\tau}\left(-\mathbf{h}_{t}+K*\text{ReLU}(\mathbf{h}_{t})+W_{\text{in}}*\mathbf{I}_{t}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Visual predictions emerge through linear reconstruction: <math id="Sx2.SSx1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{t}=W_{\text{out}}*\mathbf{h}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{I}}_{t}=W_{\text{out}}*\mathbf{h}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To integrate motor commands, we designate the first <math id="Sx2.SSx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> channels as motor-gated.
After each dynamics update, these channels are multiplicatively modulated by motor signals:</p>
<table id="Sx2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{t+1}^{(i)}=m_{i}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t+1}^{(i)}\quad\text{for }i\in\{1,\ldots,M\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐡</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mtext>for </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{t+1}^{(i)}=m_{i}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t+1}^{(i)}\quad\text{for }i\in\{1,\ldots,M\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">This implements gain modulation, the same computational principle by which posterior parietal cortex combines visual and motor signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas and Thier, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andersen et al., 1997</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx2.SSx1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Biological plausibility.</span>
We do not claim the neural field is a complete model of cortex.
Rather, it respects two cortical constraints that standard world model architectures (VAE-LSTMs, transformers, diffusion models) violate: retinotopic organization maintains spatial correspondence with visual input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wandell et al., 2007</a>)</cite>, and local lateral connectivity limits interactions to spatial neighbors.
We use ReLU as a threshold-linear approximation to spike-rate rectification, and convolutional kernels to abstract local connectivity patterns.
Regarding learning: we use backpropagation, though recent work suggests cortical circuits may implement functionally similar credit assignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lillicrap et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
Our claim concerns the computational architecture, not the specific learning mechanism.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Task Environments</h3>

<div id="Sx2.SSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx2.SSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ballistic trajectory (Experiment 1).</span>
A ball moves under gravity in a <math id="Sx2.SSx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32\times 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32\times 32</annotation></semantics></math> visual field, with random initial position and velocity.
The model observes the first 3 frames, then predicts the remainder without visual input.
Architecture: 16 channels (no motor gating).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx2.SSx2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Musculoskeletal arm (Experiments 2–3).</span>
A planar double-pendulum arm operates in a <math id="Sx2.SSx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="120\times 45" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>45</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">120\times 45</annotation></semantics></math> visual field with four motor commands following the Equilibrium-Point Hypothesis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feldman, 1986</a>)</cite>: co-contraction (C) commands control joint stiffness, reciprocal (R) commands control movement direction.
A ball falls from a random horizontal position for catching.
Architecture: 32 channels (4 motor-gated).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SSx3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Training and Evaluation</h3>

<div id="Sx2.SSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">World models are trained with mean squared prediction loss (Adam optimizer, 10,000 epochs).
For dream training (Experiment 2), we freeze the world model and train a policy network by backpropagating through the differentiable dynamics.
A separately trained catch predictor provides the learning signal; the policy maximizes predicted catch probability with gradients flowing through the frozen world model.
The trained policy deploys to real physics without fine-tuning.
Catch rate measures successful interceptions over 100 episodes.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For body schema analysis (Experiment 3), we compute a selectivity index comparing motor-gated channel activity over arm versus ball regions, normalized by reconstruction activity:</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Selectivity}=\frac{\text{Motor}_{\text{arm}}/\text{Motor}_{\text{ball}}}{\text{Recon}_{\text{arm}}/\text{Recon}_{\text{ball}}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Selectivity</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mtext>Motor</mtext><mtext>arm</mtext></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mtext>Motor</mtext><mtext>ball</mtext></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>Recon</mtext><mtext>arm</mtext></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mtext>Recon</mtext><mtext>ball</mtext></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Selectivity}=\frac{\text{Motor}_{\text{arm}}/\text{Motor}_{\text{ball}}}{\text{Recon}_{\text{arm}}/\text{Recon}_{\text{ball}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Values greater than 1 indicate body-selective representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.SSx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SSx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx2.SSx3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baseline.</span>
We compare against a VAE-LSTM inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha and Schmidhuber (2018)</a></cite>: a convolutional VAE compresses observations to a 32-dimensional latent space, an LSTM predicts latent dynamics, and a decoder reconstructs predictions.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha and Schmidhuber (2018)</a></cite>, training proceeds in two stages (VAE first for 10,000 epochs, then frozen VAE plus LSTM for 10,000 epochs) because gradients through the decoder destabilize joint training.
The neural field requires no staged training and uses 17–67<math id="Sx2.SSx3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer parameters (13K vs 850K for ballistic; 50K vs 1.7M for arm), largely because the VAE-LSTM requires dense layers connecting flattened features to latent space.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Results</h2>

<section id="Sx3.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Experiment 1: Physics from Lateral Dynamics</h3>

<figure id="Sx3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18690v1/trajectory_sequence.png" id="Sx3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/436;" width="698" height="436" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Trajectory prediction through internal dynamics. Each column shows a different ballistic trajectory (50–59 timesteps). Both models observe only the first three frames before predicting the remainder without visual input. The neural field (green) maintains smooth parabolic arcs closely tracking ground truth (gray dotted), while the VAE-LSTM (orange) exhibits erratic oscillations.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Experiment 1: Physics from Lateral Dynamics ‣ Results ‣ Neural Fields as World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows ballistic prediction: after observing a ball for three frames, activity in the neural field continues along the parabolic arc even without visual input.
During observation, a localized bump tracks the ball; remove the input, and the bump keeps moving, following learned dynamics that approximate ballistic motion.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across 10 seeds, the neural field achieves median prediction loss of
<math id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9.33\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>9.33</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.33\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> (IQR: [<math id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.000895" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.000895</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.000895</annotation></semantics></math>,
<math id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.000988" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.000988</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.000988</annotation></semantics></math>]), compared to <math id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.94\times 10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.94</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.94\times 10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>
for VAE-LSTM (p &lt; 0.001).
Beyond aggregate loss, VAE-LSTMs exhibit a failure mode that neural fields avoid.
We measured frame-to-frame displacement of predicted centroids during blind rollouts.
The neural field’s maximum displacement was 2.06 pixels, with 0.0% of sequences showing “teleportation” (jumps <math id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>3.0 pixels).
VAE-LSTM showed 21.97 pixels maximum (10.7<math id="Sx3.SSx1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger) and 15.4% teleportation (p &lt; 0.001).
Local connectivity bounds how far predictions can jump in a single timestep;
latent-space models lack this constraint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3.SSx2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Experiment 2: Dream Training Transfers</h3>

<div id="Sx3.SSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An important test for world models is whether policies trained in imagination
transfer to reality.
We freeze the trained neural field world model, then train a policy network to
catch falling balls using only the model’s prediction of the visual field.
The policy receives the neural field reconstruction as input and outputs motor commands.
Training proceeds entirely within the world model: the model generates predicted
observations, the policy generates actions, and a catch predictor (trained on real physics) scores each trajectory, with gradients flowing through the differentiable world model to the policy.
No real-environment interaction occurs during policy training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18690v1/dpmc_trajectory_sequence.png" id="Sx3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/290;" width="698" height="290" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Visuomotor prediction in the arm catching task. Both models receive motor commands throughout, but visual input only during the first three frames (Obs). Ground truth shown as gray dots. The vertical dashed line marks the transition to blind prediction.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.SSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Experiment 2: Dream Training Transfers ‣ Results ‣ Neural Fields as World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the arm task: a double pendulum controlled by muscle-like actuators must catch a falling ball.
The neural field receives motor commands alongside visual input during observation, then predicts the visual consequences of continued motor activity during the blind phase.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Policies trained within the neural field achieve 81.5% catch
rate (IQR: [79.2%, 84.7%]) when deployed to the
<span id="Sx3.SSx2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">real</span> physics environment, approaching the 89.0%
achieved by policies trained directly on real physics
(Figure <a href="#Sx3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Experiment 2: Dream Training Transfers ‣ Results ‣ Neural Fields as World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
VAE-LSTM policies achieve only 46.0%
(p = 0.003), roughly half the neural field’s performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18690v1/controller_dream_vs_real.svg" id="Sx3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/430;" width="698" height="430"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Dream training transfers to real physics. Lines show loss during dream training (right axis; plotted as catch predictor value, i.e., negated loss, so higher = better; ceiling <math id="Sx3.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>60% since the ball reaches catching distance <math id="Sx3.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≈</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx</annotation></semantics></math>40% through each episode). Points show real catch rate at evaluation (left axis). Neural field policies (green) achieve 81.5%, approaching the physics baseline (dotted). VAE-LSTM (orange) achieves comparable dream performance but shows larger sim-to-real gap.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18690v1/world_model_loss_curves.svg" id="Sx3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/257;" width="698" height="257"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Training dynamics. Neural field (green) achieves lower final loss than VAE-LSTM (orange) on the ballistic task and comparable loss on the arm task, despite using 17–67<math id="Sx3.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer parameters. Shaded regions show IQR across seeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.SSx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Prediction loss alone does not determine transfer quality: despite comparable
world model losses (Figure <a href="#Sx3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Experiment 2: Dream Training Transfers ‣ Results ‣ Neural Fields as World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), the neural field supports substantially
better policy transfer.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Why does spatial structure help?
The neural field’s dynamics function as a spatial integrator: position and
velocity are encoded directly in the topology, and the learned kernel implements
discrete integration over time.
In latent-space models, these quantities must be disentangled from a compressed
representation.
Spatial inductive bias provides a natural coordinate system for physics,
allowing the policy to exploit spatial features directly rather than learning to
decode them from an arbitrary latent space.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The neural field world model is directly interpretable in a way that
latent-space models are not.
One can watch the field dynamics unfold in each channel, observe how motor commands transform
the spatial state, and gain intuition for what the model has learned.
The ball’s predicted position is literally where activity appears in the field,
not an abstract vector requiring decoding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3.SSx3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Experiment 3: Emergent Body-Selective Encoding</h3>

<div id="Sx3.SSx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Body schema, the implicit representation of one’s own body that enables
coordinated action, has long been studied as a distinct cognitive capacity
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gallagher, 2005</a>)</cite>.
Here we find that a computational precursor to body schema can emerge as a
byproduct of visuomotor prediction.
The motor-gated architecture does not encode body versus world explicitly, it
encodes what moves contingently with motor commands.
That this corresponds to the body is discovered, not assumed.
The finding provides computational support for developmental theories proposing
that infants discover their bodies through sensorimotor contingencies
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bahrick, 1995</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rochat, 1998</a>)</cite>.
Using the arm world model, we compare motor-gated channel activity over the arm
versus the ball, normalized by reconstruction activity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18690v1/body_schema_channels.png" id="Sx3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:698/276;" width="698" height="276" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Emergent body-selective encoding in motor-gated channels. Reciprocal (R) channels show activation concentrated over the arm rather than the ball (dotted contours), despite no explicit training to distinguish body from world. Orange indicates positive activation, green negative.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.SSx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Reciprocal (R) motor channels, which control joint movement direction, show
significant arm selectivity (Figure <a href="#Sx3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Experiment 3: Emergent Body-Selective Encoding ‣ Results ‣ Neural Fields as World Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>): shoulder R median
selectivity = 2.18
(p = 0.002); elbow R median =
1.50 (p = 0.002).
These channels are approximately <math id="Sx3.SSx3.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> more active over the arm than
reconstruction alone would require.
Co-contraction (C) channels show no significant selectivity (shoulder C:
p = 0.16; elbow C: p = 0.96).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Why do R channels show selectivity while C channels do not?
The answer likely lies in visual consequences.
Reciprocal commands produce large arm movements; to predict these, the motor
channel must represent where the arm is.
Co-contraction modulates stiffness with minimal immediate visual change.
The selectivity pattern reflects what each motor command <span id="Sx3.SSx3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">does</span>.
Body selectivity emerges from the prediction objective, not explicit supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.SSx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.SSx3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Motor-gated channels reveal something deeper about how neural fields represent
dynamics.
Each channel encodes intended movement within a static spatial pattern. This
channel activation at any instant represents where the controlled object
<span id="Sx3.SSx3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">will move</span>, pixel by pixel, given the current motor command.
The same arm configuration produces
different channel patterns depending on which motor is active.
The architecture transforms temporal dynamics into spatial structure,
representing “what will move where” in the spatial pattern of the field itself.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Discussion</h2>

<div id="Sx4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We proposed that neural fields, spatially organized recurrent networks with local connectivity, offer a biologically plausible implementation of world models.
Four lines of evidence support this hypothesis.
First, the architecture aligns with known cortical organization: retinotopic structure parallels visual cortex, and motor-gated channels implement the same gain modulation found in posterior parietal cortex <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas and Thier, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andersen et al., 1997</a>)</cite>.
Animals likely learn world models by collecting sensorimotor experience and extracting predictive structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nagai, 2019</a>)</cite>.
Neural fields align with this view because spatial structure is preserved by construction rather than learned through compression.
Second, local connectivity proves sufficient to learn ballistic physics: trajectories emerge from wave-like propagation through the field, and predictions traverse intermediate locations rather than teleporting as in latent-space models (Experiment 1).
Third, the spatial structure supports effective policy learning: dream-trained policies transfer to reality with minimal sim-to-real gap (Experiment 2).
Fourth, a computational precursor to body schema emerges from visuomotor prediction alone.
Motor-gated channels spontaneously develop body-selective encoding, discovering the distinction between self and world through sensorimotor experience (Experiment 3).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Relation to prior work.</span> The neural field offers a mechanistic substrate
for the “intuitive physics engine” proposed by Battaglia et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Battaglia et al., 2013</a>)</cite>: physics emerges from learned connectivity
rather than explicit rules.
Ahuja et al. found that area MT activates during trajectory prediction even
without visual motion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahuja et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
Our neural field shows analogous behavior: during blind prediction, activity
moves through retinotopic space, providing a computational parallel to MT’s
motion representation.
Multiplicative gating by motor signals implements gain modulation, the same computational principle found in posterior parietal cortex where motor signals modulate spatially organized sensory representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salinas and Thier, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andersen et al., 1997</a>)</cite>.
Neural fields have a rich history in cognitive science through Dynamic Field Theory (DFT), which hand-specifies Amari-type dynamics to model working memory, motor planning, and decision-making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schöner et al., 2016</a>)</cite>.
Our work departs from this tradition: rather than designing field dynamics for specific cognitive functions, we learn them end-to-end from sensorimotor prediction.
The neural field discovers its own dynamics, including physics and body-selective encoding, through gradient descent on prediction error alone.
This suggests that computational principles identified by DFT may emerge naturally when spatially structured networks are trained to predict the sensory consequences of action.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Neural fields and VAE-LSTMs can achieve similar loss,
but neural fields avoid the failure mode that affects VAE-LSTMs.
Local connectivity constrains errors to smooth spatial drift. Predictions cannot
“jump” discontinuously because information must propagate through spatial
neighbors.
Latent-space models lack this constraint.
The distinction matters beyond benchmarks because architectural constraints shape how
models go wrong.
Human multiple object tracking errors arise primarily from spatial proximity. For example, when targets approach within a few degrees, crowding causes confusions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Franconeri et al., 2010</a>)</cite>.
Neural fields with local connectivity should exhibit similar proximity-dependent interference, a prediction we leave for future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implications.</span> The spontaneous emergence of body-selective encoding
suggests that self-representation does not need to be explicitly taught. Instead, it may be
computationally inevitable given the right architectural constraints.
Motor-gated channels were given only the task of action-conditional prediction and
body-selective encoding emerged as a byproduct.
One might object that this emergence is circular: given motor-gated channels, of
course they represent what moves with motor commands.
But the objection assumes the architecture succeeds at the task.
There was no guarantee that multiplicative gating would support stable learning,
that local connectivity could capture arm dynamics, or that the system would
learn accurate visuomotor prediction at all.
The emergence is not “motor channels represent the arm” but rather
“motor-gated neural fields can learn visuomotor dynamics, and when they do,
body-selective encoding follows.”</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The result demonstrates the computational sufficiency of contingency
detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bahrick and Watson, 1985</a>)</cite>: infants do not need to possess innate
knowledge of their bodies, nor require explicit teaching about self versus
world.
Given only the capacity to predict the sensory consequences of motor commands,
the distinction between self and other emerges from the statistics of
sensorimotor experience.
Infants as young as three months preferentially attend to contingent visual
feedback from their own limb movements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bahrick, 1995</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rochat, 1998</a>)</cite>. Our model shows why this attention might naturally develop
body-selective representations.
The motor-gated architecture provides a mechanistic implementation. Channels
gated by motor commands inevitably develop representations of the body because
the body is what moves contingently with those commands.
This provides a potential implementation of the comparator model of agency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blakemore et al., 2002</a>)</cite>, which proposes that the brain distinguishes self-caused from externally-caused sensations by comparing predicted sensory consequences against actual feedback.
Motor-gated channels generate action-conditional predictions; when these match observed motion, prediction error is low, while mismatch signals externally-caused motion.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Dream training connects to mental practice in motor learning.
Grush’s emulation theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grush, 2004</a>)</cite> proposes that the brain
constructs internal models (emulators) that can be run offline to simulate
action outcomes.
During overt movement, these emulators run in parallel with actual sensorimotor
loops; during imagery, they run alone.
Our neural field functions as such an emulator, a learned forward model that
predicts sensory consequences of motor commands.
Dream training succeeds because the emulator is accurate enough that policies
trained offline transfer to reality.
The documented benefits of mental practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeannerod, 1995</a>)</cite> are
consistent with this view: rehearsal within an accurate world model improves
real-world performance because imagery engages the same predictive machinery as
execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">These results also speak to the format of spatial representation.
Latent-space models function as descriptive systems. They compress experience
into abstract codes where spatial relationships are discarded and must be
reconstructed through decoding.
A gap opens between the structure of the world and the structure of the
representation.
Isomorphic world models are constitutive, meaning that representation and world share
geometric form.
To predict a trajectory is to propagate activity through space; to represent
position is to activate a location.
This aligns with enactivist accounts of perception
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">O’Regan and Noë, 2001</a>)</cite>, where understanding arises from mastery of
sensorimotor contingencies rather than construction of internal pictures.
Experiment 3 illustrates this point directly. The motor-gated channels learn not a
symbol for “arm” but the sensorimotor contingency itself. They encode what changes when a particular action is commanded.
The format of the representation already contains the spatial answer, which may
explain why physical reasoning feels immediate rather than inferential.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitations and future directions.</span>
While we implement an isomorphic world model using neural fields, the observed benefits—stable policy gradients, successful dream-to-real transfer, and emergent body schema—likely arise from the isomorphic constraint itself (preserving sensory topology) rather than the specific dynamical system.
Any architecture maintaining spatial structure should exhibit similar
properties.
The class of isomorphic world models includes ConvLSTMs, cellular automata,
graph neural networks on spatial graphs, or any architecture where latent states
preserve spatial adjacency.
Similarly, motor gating is one mechanism for integrating action into isomorphic world models, though other approaches that modulate spatial dynamics based on motor commands could serve the same function.
We view motor-gated neural fields as perhaps the simplest implementation; their established use in cognitive modeling makes them a natural starting point.
Future work should verify this hypothesis by benchmarking the broader class of
spatially-structured architectures, including motor-gated ConvLSTMs and cellular
automata, to identify which architectural choices matter most for physics
prediction.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Our demonstrations involve simple 2D
environments.
Scaling to richer scenes poses challenges that point toward future
architectures.
Object interaction, including occlusion, collision, and support, may require
representing objects in separate layers with gated interactions, allowing
objects to move independently while still influencing each other through learned
coupling.
More fundamentally, isomorphism does not need to mean pixel-isomorphism: the neural
field could operate in a three-dimensional coordinate system that preserves the
spatial structure of physical space rather than retinal space.
There is biological precedent: hippocampal place cells represent volumetric 3D
space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grieves et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and parietal area V6A encodes reaching targets
in depth coordinates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hadjidimitrakis et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.
Visual input could project into this volumetric representation, and dynamics
would unfold in a space where depth is explicit.
Such an architecture would remain isomorphic in the sense that
matters, preserving spatial adjacency in the physical world, while handling
the projective distortions that make 2D pixel space a poor model of 3D physics.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitive physics supports but does not exhaust physical reasoning.
Humans can also reason symbolically about physics, applying laws and making
deductions.
How neural field world models might interface with more abstract reasoning
systems remains an open question.
The architecture we propose handles the fast, automatic physics simulation that
supports perception and action; explicit physical reasoning may require
additional mechanisms.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx4.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx4.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx4.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conclusion.</span> Perhaps the brain predicts where the ball will land the same way it perceives where the ball is now: through spatially organized activity that propagates according to learned dynamics.
If so, intuitive physics and body schema are not separate capacities but natural consequences of predicting the sensory effects of action within a retinotopic map.</p>
</div>
</section>
